title: NAND-tree evaluation: deterministic 2^h leaf reads vs randomized ((1+sqrt 33)/4)^h expected
problem_statement: Given query access to the N = 2^h leaf bits of a complete binary tree of height h whose internal nodes compute NAND(x, y) = NOT(x AND y), compute the value of the root. Cost = number of leaf reads (queries), worst case over inputs; for a randomized algorithm, the worst case over inputs of the expected number of reads. Algorithms must always be correct (zero error).

input.parameter: n = h = height of the tree; N = 2^h leaves.
input.size_measure: Query model: the cost is the number of leaf reads. The harness materialises the N leaf bits so that reads can be counted. In the input size N, the costs read N vs Theta(N^0.7537).

algorithms.name: deterministic left-first evaluation
algorithms.idea: Evaluate the left subtree first; if it is 0 the node is 1 and the right subtree is skipped, otherwise the node is NOT(right).
algorithms.pseudocode: eval(node): if leaf: read it; if eval(left) == 0: return 1; return 1 - eval(right)
algorithms.time_complexity: 2^h = N leaf reads in the worst case (exactly 2^h on inputs where every node of value 1 has its 0-child on the right), which is optimal for deterministic algorithms (lower_bounds)
algorithms.correctness: NAND(0, y) = 1 and NAND(1, y) = NOT y, so short-circuiting on a 0 left child is exact. Worst case: a value-0 node needs both children (both are 1), and a value-1 node whose left child is 1 needs its right child too, so on the right-zero reluctant input every leaf is read (D(h) = 2 D(h-1)). Optimality (adversary argument, proved here by induction on the height; not checked against a published proof): answer every leaf query with 1 while its sibling subtree is unfinished, which leaves the parent undetermined since NAND(1, y) = NOT y; when the last leaf of a node's two subtrees is queried, choose the answer that gives that node whichever value the adversary wants for it as a 'virtual leaf' one level up. By induction on the height, every node stays undetermined until the last leaf below it is read, and its value can then still be chosen: while both subtrees of a node are unfinished, each can still take either value, so the node can be 0 (both children 1) or 1 (a child 0); once one subtree has finished, with value 1, the node equals the negation of the other subtree, which is still open, and the answer to that subtree's last leaf fixes the node to the value wanted. So any deterministic algorithm reads all 2^h leaves.

algorithms.name: randomized random-order evaluation
algorithms.idea: At every node, evaluate the two subtrees in a uniformly random order and short-circuit as above (Snir's directional algorithm, shown optimal by Saks and Wigderson 1986). Always correct; only the number of reads is random.
algorithms.pseudocode: eval(node): if leaf: read it; (a, b) = children in random order; if eval(a) == 0: return 1; return 1 - eval(b)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(((1 + sqrt(33))/4)^h) = Theta(N^0.7537) expected leaf reads in the worst case (((1 + sqrt 33)/4 ~ 1.6861; log2 of it ~ 0.7537)
algorithms.correctness: Same short-circuit rule as the deterministic algorithm, so the answer is always correct (zero error). Expected cost (derived here): on 'reluctant' inputs (value-0 nodes have two 1-children, value-1 nodes exactly one 0-child) R0(h) = 2 R1(h-1) and R1(h) = R0(h-1) + R1(h-1)/2, R0(0) = R1(0) = 1, since a value-1 node reads its 0-child first with probability 1/2. The matrix [[0, 2], [1, 1/2]] has eigenvalues (1 +- sqrt 33)/4, so R(h) = Theta(((1 + sqrt 33)/4)^h). Reluctant inputs are the worst case for this algorithm: by induction over h, a value-1 node with two 0-children costs only R0(h-1), less than R0(h-1) + R1(h-1)/2, and subtrees are independent. Saks & Wigderson 1986 prove that this is optimal for zero-error randomized algorithms (lower_bounds).

lower_bounds.bound: 2^h = N leaf reads in the worst case
lower_bounds.source: Adversary argument proved in this entry by induction on the height (deterministic algorithm, correctness field); not checked against a published proof

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(((1 + sqrt(33))/4)^h) = Omega(N^0.7537) expected leaf reads in the worst case, for ZERO-ERROR (Las Vegas) randomized algorithms; matched by the randomized algorithm here
lower_bounds.setting: query (decision-tree) model, unconditional. Bounded-error (Monte Carlo) algorithms are not covered by this statement here.
lower_bounds.source: Saks & Wigderson 1986 (statement as summarised by secondary sources found by web search, e.g. the Boolean Zoo page 'Iterated nand' and arXiv:1506.06399; the paper's text was not read)

relationship: Randomisation lowers the exponent: N leaf reads for every deterministic algorithm vs Theta(N^0.7537) expected reads for the best zero-error randomized algorithm, both proven optimal in their models (lower_bounds). Primary T4 (randomized vs deterministic, same problem, same query model); secondary T3 because, in the input size N, the improvement is polynomial to a smaller polynomial (RESEARCH_LOG RL-042 proposal, adopted here).

sources.title: Probabilistic Boolean decision trees and the complexity of evaluating game trees
sources.venue: 27th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS 1986), 29-38

verification.method: V1: both algorithms agree with an independent oracle (harness.check: full bottom-up evaluation of every node, level by level) on random leaf vectors and on reluctant inputs with random sides and random root values, h = 0..12 and 14, 16 (left-first up to 12), 4 trials each. The randomized algorithm is zero-error, so its answers are deterministic facts, not probabilistic; the validator seeds its coins. V2 (measure 'reported'): the cost is the exact number of leaf reads, counted by an instrumented leaf sequence in the harness while the implementations run unchanged, on the right-zero reluctant input with root value 1 (worst case for both). Left-first: exactly 2^h reads (h = 0..16 checked), alpha = 1.000 against 2^h at tolerance 0.02 (rivals lambda^h and h 2^h rejected). Randomized: mean of 200 seeded runs per h; alpha = 0.995 against lambda^h, lambda = (1 + sqrt 33)/4 (rivals 2^h 0.750, 1.5^h, h lambda^h rejected). Tolerance 0.05 for the randomized fit is justified in experiments/2026-10-07b_nand_tree_counts.py: the EXACT expectations (recurrence) give alpha = 0.998 on these h (the lower-order eigenvalue (1 - sqrt 33)/4 ~ -1.186 contributes 0.002), and over 40 alternative seed sets the 200-sample fit has alpha mean 0.997, sd 0.005, range 0.989-1.008. The validator-seeded sample means lie within 2.0 standard errors of the exact expectations at every h. The rival 2^h is 0.25 away.

caveats: The randomized V2 fit uses sample means (200 per h), so its alpha is a statistical estimate; it is reproducible because the validator seeds every run. Uniformly random leaves are much easier than reluctant inputs for both algorithms, so V2 uses the worst-case family. The randomized lower bound quoted is for zero-error algorithms (as summarised from Saks & Wigderson 1986 by secondary sources); this entry makes no claim about bounded-error algorithms. The deterministic lower bound rests on the adversary argument proved here (not checked against a published proof).
notes: Quantum algorithms evaluate NAND trees with about sqrt(N) queries (Farhi, Goldstone & Gutmann 2008 and follow-up work); that line is not recorded here because the source could not be checked by title (Crossref stores no title for doi:10.4086/toc.2008.v004a008). A T9 extension would need a verified quantum algorithm and the classical randomized lower bound above.
